title: Diaper Math
text: Four diapers left. {kid} goes through six a day. You do the math, and the math says Wednesday at noon.

choices.label: Order now. Survive the size chart.

outcomes.text: Size 4 is "22–37 lbs." Size 5 is "27+ lbs." {kid} is 31 pounds and therefore both. You buy the box marked "Overnight" because you'd like some of that too.
Done in four taps. Three days later you learn you've subscribed to a box every nine days, forever, with no visible way out. The diapers have you now.
"on it 👍" You brace for pull-ups. At 6:12 PM a photo arrives: right size, right box, receipt. Who is this person?
Read 2:14 PM. No reply. At dinner {partner} asks, "Did you get diapers?" The diapers remain theoretical.
Four is plenty. Four is a number. Nothing bad has ever happened with four.

title: Fourteen Questions
text: Brynn's RSVP form for Juniper's party has 14 questions. Number 6 is allergies. Number 9 is your child's "party energy, 1 to 5." Number 14 says, "Tell us about your family!"

outcomes.text: Allergies: none. Party energy: 5, unfortunately. Number 14 takes eleven minutes and a second draft. Brynn replies at once: "LOVE this 💛"
You hit submit. A second form arrives: "Volunteer Sign-Up (optional!!)." It is not optional. You're on cupcakes.
It goes through. Brynn texts: "Just confirming!! 'No' for number of kids attending?" You fix it. Your row has a comment on it now.
It goes through clean. Nobody reads number 14 anyway, except Brynn, who reads every one of them twice.
Four minutes. Under "Tell us about your family!" {partner} has written, "We're very tired." Brynn replies: "SAME 😭💛"
"Who's Brynn?" You explain Brynn. {partner} is quiet for a long time. "I'm not doing that." Fair.
Maybe is a legal status. Maybe means you haven't checked with your toddler's nap. Maybe can last forever.

title: Three Pages
text: The fire station field-trip form is due tomorrow at 9. It's three pages. It wants a signature, two emergency contacts, and your child's "comfort item and backup comfort item."

choices.label: Fill in all three pages properly

outcomes.text: Emergency contact #2 can't live with the child. You write down your neighbor Dale, whose last name you have never known. "Dale (next door)." It's a legal document now.
Comfort item: Bun-Bun. Backup comfort item: you look around the room for a while and write "also Bun-Bun." Signed. It's the most honest document you've ever filed.
The closest pen is a purple crayon. The second closest is the TV remote. You sign a three-page legal document in purple crayon. Daycare doesn't even blink.
The closest pen is a pen. You can't believe it either. Signed, folded and in the backpack in ninety seconds. It will never happen again.
{partner} reads all three pages and catches that you listed the vet as your pediatrician. You don't have a pet. Signed, fixed, in the backpack.
"Can't it wait?" It can't. It does anyway. The form goes back on the fridge, gaining power.
That's the whole point of a form. It goes back on the fridge, under a drawing of either you or a potato.

title: Press 9 for More Options
text: The pediatrician's phone tree. Press 1 for appointments. Press 2 for prescriptions. Press 7 to hear these options again, slower, as if you're the problem. Nothing for "rash."

outcomes.text: You are caller number 6. Then caller number 7. Someone has cut in line on a phone. At minute 22, Nurse Pat: "Send a photo. Sounds like eczema. Fragrance-free cream twice a day." You could cry.
The second a human answers, {kid} yells "I'M NAKED" from the next room. Accurate. Nurse Pat makes a note, says "eczema, cream twice a day," and never brings it up.
Password reset. A code, sent to an email you made in 2009. A second code. A photo upload. Two hours later: "Looks like eczema. Cream twice daily." Served by a portal. Who knew.
The portal wants a new password with a symbol, a number and a capital letter, not one of your last twelve. You've used every password there is. The portal wins.

choices.label: Ask {partner} to call on their break

outcomes.text: They call from a stairwell at work. "Eczema. Cream twice a day. Nurse Pat says hi." You've never met Nurse Pat. You love Nurse Pat.
"Can't, back-to-backs all day." The rash and the phone tree are still yours. So, somehow, is the pan-flute hold music, in your head.
It's probably fine. You check it every eleven minutes for the rest of the day, just to make sure it's still fine.

title: Possession Is Nine-Tenths
text: The library books are due tomorrow. {kid} has seen you looking at them and is now lying face down on the stack, saying "MY books" into the carpet.

choices.label: Make it an outing. They get to work the slot.

outcomes.text: The drop slot takes the books one at a time while {kid} says "bye, book" to each one. They check out four new ones. The cycle of ownership continues.
At the slot, {kid} won't let go of the last one. A librarian kneels and explains due dates, very seriously, one professional to another. They hand it over.
Renewed. New due date: next Friday. You've bought a week, which is the most anyone can buy.
The site asks you to select every square with a bus. You fail. It asks for crosswalks. You fail. The library has decided you're a robot. It isn't wrong.
At 12:40 PM: a photo of the drop slot, captioned "you sneak." Returned. Respected.
{partner} finds them at the office and, as a courtesy, brings them home again. The books have now commuted.
{kid} wins the property dispute by lying on it. The books stay. You'll deal with it tomorrow, which is also the deadline.

title: There Are No Diapers
text: Your hand reaches into the diaper box and touches cardboard. The worst texture in the world. {kid} is wearing the last diaper, and the last diaper is on a clock.

choices.label: Drive to the store. With {kid}. In pajama pants.

outcomes.text: They have every size but yours. You buy the next one up. {kid} rides in the cart announcing "DIAPERS" to strangers, who agree: diapers.
In, out and home in 31 minutes, a personal record, set in pajama pants. {kid} falls asleep in the car seat on the way back. You'll pay for that nap at bedtime.

choices.label: Knock on Dale's door. Dale has grandkids.

outcomes.text: Dale has diapers. Dale's grandkid is four months old. You walk home with six size 1s, each the size of a sandwich. On {kid}, they're more of a suggestion.
Dale comes back with one cloth diaper from 1987 and two safety pins. Neither of you knows how it works. You figure it out together, on Dale's porch, in silence.
{partner} walks out of a meeting, says "family thing" in a voice that ends questions, and shows up 40 minutes later with diapers and a coffee you needed.
"In a meeting till 4." It's 12:10. You do the math again. It's worse the second time.

title: No Form, No Truck
text: Daycare is closed for pink eye. Daycare's email is not. Subject: "FIRE STATION TRIP: FINAL CALL." The trip is tomorrow. The form is still on your fridge.

choices.label: Grovel by email. Use the word "unprecedented."

outcomes.text: You write 340 words. You use "unprecedented" once and "so sorry" four times. The reply: "This once." You will owe this person forever.
"Rules are rules," the director replies, in a font that feels personal. Tomorrow, {kid} stays behind with the assistant director and a bin of puzzles.
A parent who comes along doesn't need a form. So tomorrow you'll spend four hours with eleven toddlers in plastic fire hats. That's the price of one signature.

choices.label: Let it go. It's just a truck.

outcomes.text: It isn't just a truck. Tomorrow the group chat will post 23 photos of other people's toddlers in fire hats. You'll scroll through every one, slowly, as penance.

title: Brynn Is Following Up
text: The RSVP for Juniper's party was due at 5. It is no longer before 5.

messages.text: hiiii!! finalizing the headcount for Juniper's party 🎈
still need yours! it was due at 5 🙂

outcomes.text: Late RSVPs bring the ice. Nobody told you this rule. It's the oldest rule there is.
Brynn will not see what Brynn can do. You can tell from the smiley, which has been through a lot today.

chat.text: headcount already went in 🙂 i'll see what i can do 🙂

outcomes.text: Three smileys, each one a little colder than the last.

chat.text: oh weird! it was paper 🙂 in the cubby 🙂 with a ribbon 🙂

choices.label: Leave it on read. Brynn might forget.

outcomes.text: Brynn does not forget. Brynn has a spreadsheet with conditional formatting. Your row is red. Somehow, at the party, your row will still be red.

title: After Hours
text: The pediatrician's office closed at 5. The rash did not. It's on both elbows now, plus the back of one knee, and you have 31 browser tabs open about it.

choices.label: Call the after-hours line. Settle in.

outcomes.text: Forty-six minutes on hold. Then a nurse with a voice like a warm blanket says eczema, fragrance-free cream, call Monday. You say thank you four times and mean every one.
The nurse wants them seen tonight, to be safe. Urgent care: eleven people ahead of you, nine of them coughing. A doctor looks for forty seconds. "Eczema." Copay: $75.

choices.label: Post a photo in the group chat

outcomes.text: Dev's mom is a pediatric nurse. "Eczema. Fragrance-free cream. Call Monday if it spreads." Right, kind, fast. And now 22 parents have seen your child's knee.
Forty replies in nine minutes: eczema, allergies, "have you tried celery juice," a photo of somebody else's rash. You call the nurse line anyway, an hour behind.
They didn't. You didn't. You both look at the rash like it's a third parent who was supposed to handle this. Then you call the nurse line, not speaking.

title: Final Overdue Notice (Final)
text: Friday, 5 PM. The library has frozen your card until the books come back. Story time is tomorrow. Story time is the one hour a week {kid} sits still.

choices.label: Race them over before the 6 PM close

outcomes.text: 5:52 PM. You slide the books across the desk, panting. {kid} says "thank you, library." The librarian waives the fine and unfreezes the card. Worth every step.
5:59 PM. The door locks as your hand touches it. Through the glass, a librarian points at the hours sign and mouths, "Monday."

choices.label: Pay the fine online and call it even

outcomes.text: $16.80, plus a $2 fee for the convenience of paying it. The card stays frozen until the books come back, which they won't, because they're furniture now.

choices.label: Keep them. Start a home library.

outcomes.text: You declare the books part of the household's permanent collection. The library sends a $68 replacement bill. Your account has gone to collections, in both senses.
